newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban's French prisoners say waiting but well.
newsitem.headline: Taleban's French prisoners say waiting but well.

text.p: Two French aid workers held in Kabul by Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia said on Thursday they were in good health and appreciated the messages of support they had received.
"Our health is okay and we started receiving visits yesterday," said Jose Daniel Llorente, interviewed by Reuters in the cell he shares with Frederic Michel.
A senior Taleban official was present throughout the brief interview, which was conducted in English.
The two Frenchmen, who work for the private Paris-based charity Action Contre la Faim (Action Against Hunger), were detained along with five Afghan staffers last week.
Taleban officials say they are under investigation for "immoral deeds" in connection with a lunch given by ACF's women expatriate staff for Afghan women working for the group.
The Taleban say that the men were at the party in the presence of the unveiled Afghan women, an accusation that ACF witnesses deny.
Armed Taleban fighters raided the ACF compound during the lunch. They later went to a U.N. compound and detained the Frenchmen, both of whom say they had not been at the lunch.
In the raid, the Taleban seized a number of cameras, photographs, compact discs and magazines as evidence.
The remaining seven ACF international staff left Kabul for Pakistan shortly after the arrests.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September last year from forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and now control more than two thirds of Afghanistan, have vowed to implement strict Islamic Sharia law throughout the country.
The United Nations and the French government have urged the Taleban to release the Frenchmen immediately.
The militia's minister of information said on Thursday the Taleban would not bow to international pressure.
"We will only obey the rules that Islam dictates," Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters.
Llorente had been posted to Afghanistan just one week before his arrest. Michel had been working in Kabul for two months.
Looking clean and relaxed, Michel said they had not been maltreated. "We have had good treatment and for the moment we don't need anything. We are just waiting, but that is okay," he said.
The two men said they had been visited by the International Committee of the Red Cross, a French diplomat and several fellow aid workers, who brought food, books, cigarettes and toiletries.
"We would like to thank everyone for all the messages we have received, and for thinking of us," said Michel.
The Frenchmen are occupying a room four metres (yards) by five on the first floor of a prison block in the grounds of the Ministry of Accountability -- formerly the Ministry of National Security.
Their cell has bars on the window and a thin wooden door, which was not locked during the interview. The room has cushions on the floor and a wood-burning stove.
The aid workers are allowed to walk in the small yard outside the prison for a few hours each day.
No information is available on the fate of the five jailed Afghan workers.
